extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mineralogy/crystallography and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopaedic summary of crystalline properties: optical, thermal, magnetic/electrical, and relations between crystalline form and chemical composition, with definitions, experimental observations and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichroism / Dichroic crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniaxial (tetragonal and hexagonal) crystals showing perceptible differences in colour for the ordinary and extraordinary rays are said to be 'dichroic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: a plate of tourmaline cut parallel to the principal axis can produce polarized light; two such plates crossed form a polarizer/analyser. Use of a dichroscope or removal of the analyser in a polarizing microscope can separate axial colours. Example diagnostic use: distinguishing ruby (dichroic) from spinel-ruby (isotropic, not dichroic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleochroism / Trichroism in biaxial crystals
rubrics_metrics.description: In biaxial (orthorhombic, monoclinic and anorthic) crystals, rays vibrating along each of the three principal vibration-directions may be differently absorbed and, in coloured crystals, differently coloured; such crystals are 'trichroic' or in general 'pleochroic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Face colours may be mixtures of two axial colours; to observe axial colours separately use a dichroscope or a polarizing microscope without the analyser. Example: iolite shows markedly different colours when viewed along three perpendicular directions (dark blue, pale blue, pale yellow). Dichroscope construction and use are described (calcite rhombohedron with glass prisms, lens, aperture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dichroscope (instrument) use for pleochroism
rubrics_metrics.description: The dichroscope (or dichroiscope) consists of a calcite cleavage rhombohedron with cemented glass prisms and a viewing aperture; the observer sees two images which reveal differing colours for pleochroic crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate the crystal relative to the instrument to find maximum colour difference when vibration directions in the crystal coincide with those in the calcite. Especially useful for examining faceted gemstones, even mounted ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular polarization in crystals (optical activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some optically isotropic and uniaxial crystals can rotate the plane of polarization of light; in uniaxial crystals this occurs for light transmitted along the optic axis, while in isotropic (cubic) crystals all directions may show rotatory action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition: crystals that crystallize in symmetry-classes without planes or centres of symmetry (enantiomorphous / hemihedral forms: right- and left-handed). Examples: cubic—sodium chlorate/bromate/uranyl acetate; tetragonal—strychnine sulphate, guanidine carbonate; rhombohedral—quartz, cinnabar; hexagonal—potassium lithium sulphate. Note: rotatory power may be lost on dissolution (except some cases like strychnine sulphate), indicating differing causes (spiral crystal arrangement vs molecular structure). The phenomenon can be imitated by a spiral pile of mica plates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical anomalies of crystals (exceptions and causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions exist to general relations between external form and optical properties (e.g., cubic external form but doubly refracting internally), termed 'optical anomalies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed causes include internal strains from cooling or earth pressures, and mimetic twinning leading to higher external symmetry (pseudo-cubic forms). Some anomalies arise from phase-transformations preserving external form. Historical and literature references provided (e.g., Mallard, Brauns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anisotropy of thermal conductivity and isothermal surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals transmit heat rays and can doubly refract them; surfaces expressing conductivity and dilatation reflect the same symmetry as optical ellipsoids: spheroid for uniaxial, sphere for cubic, and ellipsoid for biaxial crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: melt patterns in wax on quartz plates cut parallel and perpendicular to the principal axis produce circle vs ellipse. Consequence: coefficients of thermal expansion differ by direction (uniaxial: two principal coefficients; biaxial: three), so non-cubic crystals change face angles slightly with temperature (example: rhombohedral angle of calcite decreases by 8'37" from 0 to 100°C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anisotropy of magnetic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystals may be paramagnetic or diamagnetic and (except cubic) show direction-dependent induced magnetization; a sphere of crystal in a magnetic field will orient so its principal axis is parallel or perpendicular to the field depending on magnetic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnetic-character surfaces: spheroid in uniaxial, sphere in cubic, ellipsoid in orthorhombic/monoclinic/anorthic — analogous relation to optical and thermal ellipsoids. Orientation depends on whether the principal axis is direction of maximum or minimum magnetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dielectric and electrical conductivity anisotropy
rubrics_metrics.description: Dielectric constants of non-conducting crystals and electrical conductivity of crystals vary with direction and may be represented by sphere/spheroid/ellipsoid surfaces analogous to optical/thermal properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sphere of crystal in an electromagnetic field will align so the axis of maximum induction is parallel to field lines. Examples: in rhombohedral haematite conductivity along principal axis is half that perpendicular; in rhombohedral bismuth conductivities are in ratio 1.6:1. Conducting crystals are thermo-electric and show direction-dependent thermo-electric force (examples with pyrites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermo-electric and pyro-/piezo-electric phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Conducting crystals can be thermo-electric; in certain non-centrosymmetric crystals changes of temperature produce pyroelectric charges and changes of pressure along uniterminal axes produce piezo-electric effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pyroelectricity condition: crystals with no centre of symmetry and with uniterminal (polar) axes; heating reverses polarity labels ('analogous' vs 'antilogous' pole). Examples: tourmaline, quartz (alternate edges of prism become charged), boracite, hemimorphite, tartaric acid, cane-sugar. Charge distribution can be visualized by dusting a sieved mixture of red-lead (positive) and sulphur (negative): red-lead attracted to negative areas, sulphur to positive, mapping charges. Piezo-electric charges mirror pyroelectric distribution when pressure applied along uniterminal axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimorphism, trimorphism, polymorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances identical in chemical composition but crystallizing in different forms are 'dimorphous' (two forms), 'trimorphous' (three forms), or more generally 'polymorphic' (multiple forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: carbon — diamond (cubic) vs graphite (hexagonal) with vastly different physical properties; CaCO3 as calcite vs aragonite; HgI2 as red tetragonal vs yellow orthorhombic. Polymorphism has profound effects on physical properties (hardness, conductivity, density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homoeomorphism (similar form, different chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemically distinct substances may exhibit similarity of crystalline form; such substances are termed 'homoeomorphous.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: iodyrite (AgI), greenockite (CdS), and zincite (ZnO) have practically identical crystalline form; other pairings listed (calcite and sodium nitrate, celestite and marcasite). Such similarities may be accidental or informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism and isomorphous series
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemically related substances frequently crystallize in similar forms (isomorphous); members of an isomorphous series share forms, cleavages, optical characters, and small differences in angles (usually within 1–2°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isomorphous series often allow mutual replacement of equivalent elements (solid solution), producing 'mixed crystals' or isomorphous mixtures. Examples: rhombohedral carbonates with formula R"CO3 where R" = Ca, Mg, Fe, Mn, Zn, Co, Pb (calcite group); sulphates/selenates of K, Rb, Cs among salts. Isomorphism is important for classifying minerals and predicting substitutional chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isodimorphism and related double salts / hydration states
rubrics_metrics.description: Isodimorphism: members of a chemical family may exist in two distinct crystal systems (isodimorphous groups). Additionally, related compounds often form double salts or crystallize with different amounts/kinds of crystallization molecules (water, alcohol), producing distinct crystallographic substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: carbonates with R"CO3 where different R" give orthorhombic vs rhombohedral forms; arsenic and antimony trioxides each occur in cubic and monoclinic/orthorhombic forms (arsenolite/claudetite, senarmontite/valentinite) that are isomorphous in cleavage and angles. Double salts and hydration states (e.g., sodium sulfate with 0, 7 or 10 waters) produce crystallographically distinct substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphotropic relations (chemical substitution altering axes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacement of atoms or radicals in a molecule by others can alter crystalline form or selectively change axial ratios and dimensions — a 'morphotropic' relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: successive substitution in benzene derivatives alters axial ratios (table given for benzene, resorcin, picric acid); humite group shows progressive addition of Mg2SiO4 increasing length of vertical axis. Morphotropy describes systematic trends in crystal morphology driven by chemical substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-effect (insensitivity of form to substitution in large molecules)
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex, high-molecular-weight molecules, replacement of some atoms by others may produce little or no influence on crystalline form because the 'mass effect' of the molecule dominates isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: alunite group where Na or K can be replaced by Pb without much change; tourmaline shows wide compositional variation but little variation in crystalline form. This concept qualifies expectations of isomorphism in large-molecule systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic axes as superior comparative metric for crystal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: For comparing crystalline forms of isomorphous and morphotropic substances, 'topic axes' calculated from axial ratios and molecular volume give a more accurate comparison than quoting angles or axial ratios alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topic axes express relative molecular distances in axial directions and allow finer, more physically meaningful comparisons between related crystals (recommended when precise comparison is needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enantiomorphous crystallization of optical isomers
rubrics_metrics.description: Optical isomers (enantiomers) such as the two isomerides of tartaric acid crystallize in related but enantiomorphous forms (right- and left-handed crystal forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: crystallographic form can reflect molecular chirality; enantiomorphous crystals may exhibit opposite optical rotation in solution or different rotatory behaviour in the crystalline state.
